common_name: Nastarana Rose (Fragrant White Noisette-Type Musk Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Nastarana is a musk-scented antique rose of Persian origin that can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Nastarana, an antique rose of Persian origin also known as the Musk Cluster Rose, bears clusters of small, single to semi-double, pure white flowers with a strong, sweet musk fragrance that carries well through the garden, especially in the evening. It flowers repeatedly from late spring through fall on long, somewhat lax canes that can be grown as a large informal shrub or trained as a short climber against a fence or arbor. Tough and adaptable, it tolerates heat, poor soil, and general neglect far better than many modern roses, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood to stay productive and shapely.

common_name: Kronprinzessin Viktoria Rose (White Sport of Souvenir de la Malmaison)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Kronprinzessin Viktoria is a white-flowered sport of the classic Bourbon rose Souvenir de la Malmaison, sharing its quartered flower form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Kronprinzessin Viktoria, introduced in 1888 as a white-flowered sport of the beloved Bourbon rose Souvenir de la Malmaison, bears large, flat, quartered blooms in creamy white sometimes touched with the faintest blush, carrying the same rich, classic Bourbon fragrance as its famous parent. It reblooms in flushes through the growing season on a compact, well-branched shrub, though like its parent it can struggle in prolonged wet weather, which sometimes causes buds to ball and fail to open fully. Feed and water a bit more generously than tougher rose classes, and prune lightly after each bloom flush to encourage continued rebloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Camaieux is a striped Gallica rose whose petals open deep pink-purple striped with white and fade toward soft gray-lavender.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Camaieux tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. Introduced in 1830, it bears semi-double flowers that open a striking deep pink-purple irregularly striped with white, gradually fading through soft mauve to a hazy gray-lavender as the blooms age, giving a single plant several color effects across its bloom period. Like other Gallicas it flowers once in a heavy late-spring flush with a strong old-rose fragrance, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering.

common_name: Duc de Guiche Rose (Deep Magenta-Purple Quartered Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Duc de Guiche bears large, fully double, quartered blooms in deep magenta-purple.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Duc de Guiche tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. It bears large, fully double flowers that open a rich crimson-magenta and deepen toward purple as they age, arranged in the neatly quartered, old-rose form prized by collectors, with a strong, classic fragrance. Like other Gallicas it blooms once in a spectacular heavy flush in late spring, then rests for the remainder of the season. It is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy, needing only routine removal of dead or crossing wood after flowering to stay vigorous and well-shaped.

common_name: Belle de Crécy Rose (Classic Mauve-Pink Aging to Gray-Violet Gallica)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown, own-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Belle de Crécy is one of the most celebrated Gallica roses, known for its unusual color-shifting blooms.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Belle de Crécy tolerates leaner soil and more neglect than modern hybrid tea roses, in keeping with its heritage as a tough antique Gallica. Introduced before 1848, it bears fully double, richly fragrant flowers that open a warm mauve-pink and gradually shift through the bloom period toward a smoky gray-violet, an unusual and much-admired color transformation that has made it one of the most sought-after Gallica roses among collectors. Its rather lax, arching canes benefit from light support or underplanting to keep the heavy flowers from touching the ground. Like other Gallicas it blooms once in a spectacular late-spring flush, then rests for the remainder of the season, and is notably disease-resistant and cold-hardy.
